topic: why a mapping function is needed
prompt: Why is a cache mapping function needed at all?

options.text: Because there are fewer cache lines than main memory blocks
Because there are more cache lines than main memory blocks
Because blocks and lines are different sizes
Because the cache is volatile

explanation: Far fewer lines than blocks, so some rule has to decide which blocks may occupy which lines.

why.a: Correct. Far fewer lines than blocks, so some rule has to decide which blocks may occupy which lines.
why.b: Wrong, and if it were true no mapping would be needed at all.
why.c: Wrong. A block occupies a line, so they are the same size.
why.d: Wrong. Volatility has nothing to do with placement.

topic: why a mapping function is needed
prompt: There are {{1}} cache lines than main memory blocks, so a mapping function is needed.
explanation: Fewer. The memory deck writes it as m much less than M.

prompt: Select the three techniques for mapping blocks into cache lines.

options.text: Direct
Associative
Set associative
Sequential

explanation: Direct, associative, set associative. Sequential is an access method, from the memory characteristics slide, not a mapping function.

why.a: Correct, and it is the simplest.
why.b: Correct, also called fully associative.
why.c: Correct, and it combines the best of the other two.
why.d: Wrong. Sequential access is what magnetic tape does.

prompt: {{1}} techniques can be used for mapping blocks into cache lines.
explanation: Three: direct, associative and set associative.

prompt: Direct mapping, the simplest technique, maps each block of main memory into:

options.text: Only one possible cache line
Any cache line
Any line within one set
Two possible cache lines

explanation: Exactly one line, which is what makes it simple and what makes thrashing possible.

why.a: Correct. Exactly one line, which is what makes it simple and what makes thrashing possible.
why.b: Wrong. That is associative mapping.
why.c: Wrong. That is set associative mapping.
why.d: Wrong. Two lines per block would be 2-way set associative.

prompt: Direct mapping is described as the {{1}} technique.
explanation: Simplest. Its advantage is that it is simple and inexpensive to implement.

prompt: In the direct mapping expression i equals j modulo m, what do the letters mean?

options.text: i is the cache line number, j is the main memory block number, m is the number of lines in the cache
i is the block number, j is the line number, m is the number of blocks
i is the tag, j is the index, m is the offset
i is the set number, j is the line number, m is the associativity

explanation: Line equals block mod line count. It is the same rule as the Cache deck's Cache Line equals Main Memory Block Number mod Number of Cache Addresses.

why.a: Correct. Line equals block mod line count.
why.b: Wrong, and it swaps i and j.
why.c: Wrong. Those are the address fields, not the formula's letters.
why.d: Wrong. Sets belong to set associative mapping.

prompt: Direct mapping is expressed as i equals j modulo m, where i is the cache {{1}} number and m is the number of {{2}} in the cache.
explanation: Line, and lines. Only j refers to main memory.

prompt: To determine whether a block is in a direct mapped cache, you:

options.text: Use the line field of the memory address to index the cache line, then compare the tag from the address with the line tag
Simultaneously compare every line's tag
Search the sets in order until a match is found
Ask main memory whether the block is cached

explanation: Index first, then compare one tag. That single comparison is why direct mapping is inexpensive.

why.a: Correct. Index first, then compare one tag.
why.b: Wrong. Comparing every tag at once is the associative method.
why.c: Wrong. Nothing is searched in order; the index goes straight to the line.
why.d: Wrong. The cache answers for itself, using its tags.

prompt: Use the {{1}} field of the memory address to index the cache line, then compare the tag from the address with the line tag.
explanation: The line field, which the Cache deck calls the index.

topic: a hit in a direct mapped cache
prompt: If the tag from the address matches the line tag, what follows?

options.text: A cache hit, and the corresponding word is retrieved from the indexed line
A cache miss, and the line is updated
The next line is checked
The cache is flushed

explanation: A hit, and the word comes from the line the index already selected.

why.a: Correct. A hit, and the word comes from the line the index already selected.
why.b: Wrong. That happens when the tags do not match.
why.c: Wrong. In direct mapping there is only one line to check.
why.d: Wrong. Flushing belongs to virtual caches at a context switch.

topic: a hit in a direct mapped cache
prompt: In a direct mapped cache, only one line ever has to be checked for a given address.
explanation: One only, because the index picks it out. That is the difference from associative mapping, which has to examine every line's tag.

why.true: Correct. The line field selects the single candidate line.
why.false: Wrong. A block can only ever be in one line, so there is nowhere else to look.

topic: a miss in a direct mapped cache
prompt: If the tags do not match, what happens?

options.text: A cache miss, and the indexed cache line is updated with the word and the tag
A cache hit, and the word is delivered
Another line is chosen to hold the block
The address is discarded

explanation: A miss, and the line is overwritten with the new word and its tag. There is no choice of line: the index already fixed it.

why.a: Correct. A miss, and the line is overwritten with the new word and its tag.
why.b: Wrong. A hit needs the tags to match.
why.c: Wrong. Choosing a line is what associative mapping has to do.
why.d: Wrong. The access still has to be served.

topic: a miss in a direct mapped cache
prompt: If both do not match, then it is a cache {{1}}, and the cache line is updated with the word and the {{2}}.
explanation: A miss, and both the word and the tag are written. Without the new tag the line would claim to hold the wrong block.

prompt: The advantage of direct mapping is that it is:

options.text: Simple and inexpensive to implement
Free of thrashing
Able to place any block anywhere
The fastest at high hit rates

explanation: Simple and inexpensive. Only one tag comparison is ever needed.

why.a: Correct. Simple and inexpensive.
why.b: Wrong, and thrashing is precisely its disadvantage.
why.c: Wrong. That freedom belongs to associative mapping.
why.d: Wrong. No such claim is made.

prompt: Direct mapping is simple and {{1}} to implement.
explanation: Inexpensive. Fully associative mapping is the costly one, since every tag must be compared at once.

prompt: What is thrashing, in the direct mapping disadvantage?

options.text: Two blocks that map to the same line being continually swapped, so the hit ratio is low
The cache being flushed at every context switch
The pipeline stalling on a data hazard
A block being written to two lines at once

explanation: Repeated references to two different blocks that map into the same line evict each other in turn, so neither is ever there when wanted.

why.a: Correct, and the deck names the effect thrashing.
why.b: Wrong. That is the virtual cache problem.
why.c: Wrong. Stalling belongs to the pipelining topic.
why.d: Wrong. A block occupies one line at a time.

prompt: The disadvantage of direct mapping is that there is a {{1}} cache location for any given block, so two blocks mapping to the same line are continually swapped and the {{2}} ratio is low.
explanation: A fixed location, and a low hit ratio. Set associative mapping was invented to address exactly this.
